/conditions/osteoarthritis/symptoms.breadcrumb: Osteoarthritis symptoms — what to look for
/conditions/osteoarthritis/symptoms.bodyHtml:
Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis in the UK, affecting around 8.5 million adults. Symptoms develop gradually as cartilage wears down in weight-bearing and high-use joints — most often the knees, hips, hands, and spine.

Common symptoms of osteoarthritis

  • Joint pain that worsens with activity and eases with rest
  • Morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes
  • Reduced range of motion in the affected joint
  • Grating or crunching sensations (crepitus)
  • Mild swelling around the joint, especially after use
  • Bony enlargements at the finger joints (Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes)

When to see your GP

Book a GP appointment if joint pain has lasted more than a few weeks, is limiting daily activities, or is accompanied by significant swelling, locking, or giving way.

faqs.q: What are the first signs of osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: The earliest signs of osteoarthritis often include joint pain, stiffness — particularly in the morning or after rest — and reduced flexibility in the affected area. Symptoms typically develop gradually, so keep a short symptom diary and speak to your GP if pain persists for more than a few weeks.

faqs.q: How is osteoarthritis diagnosed in the UK?
faqs.a: In the UK, GPs diagnose osteoarthritis from your symptoms, a clinical examination, and — where appropriate — blood tests, X-rays, ultrasound or MRI. For inflammatory types, your GP may refer you to UK healthcare rheumatology for specialist review under NICE guidance.

faqs.q: Can oa symptoms come and go?
faqs.a: Yes. Many people with oa experience flares — periods of worse pain, swelling and stiffness — followed by quieter spells. Tracking your flares helps you and your GP spot triggers and adjust treatment.

faqs.q: When should I see a GP about osteoarthritis symptoms?
faqs.a: Book a GP appointment if joint pain has lasted more than a few weeks, is interfering with sleep or daily life, or is accompanied by swelling, warmth, locking or unexplained fatigue. Early assessment leads to better long-term outcomes.

faqs.q: Is osteoarthritis the same as general arthritis pain?
faqs.a: No — there are over 100 forms of arthritis, and osteoarthritis has its own pattern of symptoms, affected joints and treatment pathway. Getting the right diagnosis matters because the most effective treatments differ between conditions.

/conditions/osteoarthritis/treatment.question: Osteoarthritis treatment options
/conditions/osteoarthritis/treatment.answer: OA cannot be cured, but evidence-based treatment significantly improves pain and function. NICE recommends a combined approach centred on exercise, weight management, and pain relief.
/conditions/osteoarthritis/treatment.bodyHtml:
OA cannot be cured, but evidence-based treatment significantly improves pain and function. NICE recommends a combined approach centred on exercise, weight management, and pain relief.

Treatment approaches

Exercise therapy

Strength training and aerobic activity reduce knee and hip pain more reliably than any other non-surgical treatment.

Weight management

Every kilogram lost reduces knee joint load by up to four kilograms during walking.

Topical NSAIDs

First-line pharmacological option for hand and knee OA per NICE 2022 guidance.

Oral NSAIDs and paracetamol

Short-term use for flare control, taken at the lowest effective dose.

Steroid injections

Short-term relief for severe flares — typically no more than three per year per joint.

Joint replacement surgery

Considered when conservative treatment no longer controls pain or function.

faqs.q: What is the best treatment for osteoarthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: UK treatment for osteoarthritis follows NICE guidance and usually combines self-management (exercise, weight control, pacing), pain relief, and — where needed — specialist medication or therapy. There is no single "best" option; the right plan depends on the type, severity and joints involved.

faqs.q: Can osteoarthritis be cured?
faqs.a: Most forms of oa cannot be cured, but they can be very effectively managed. With the right combination of exercise, medication, and lifestyle support, many people maintain a full and active life.

faqs.q: What painkillers help osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: Common options include paracetamol, topical or oral NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen) and, for inflammatory types, prescription medication such as DMARDs or biologics. Always take pain relief at the lowest effective dose and ask your GP or pharmacist about interactions.

faqs.q: Do I need a referral to see a rheumatologist for oa?
faqs.a: Yes — in the UK, you'll usually need a referral from your GP to access UK healthcare rheumatology services. If your GP suspects an inflammatory arthritis, NICE recommends urgent referral so that treatment can start early.

faqs.q: Are there free UK healthcare resources for osteoarthritis treatment?
faqs.a: Yes. UK healthcare physiotherapy, occupational therapy, pain clinics and self-management programmes are available — many free at the point of use. Ask your GP or check the UK healthcare system website for services in your area.

/conditions/osteoarthritis/exercises.question: Best exercises for osteoarthritis
/conditions/osteoarthritis/exercises.answer: Movement is the single most effective self-management tool for OA. Combine low-impact aerobic activity with strength work targeting the muscles around affected joints.
/conditions/osteoarthritis/exercises.bodyHtml:
Movement is the single most effective self-management tool for OA. Combine low-impact aerobic activity with strength work targeting the muscles around affected joints.

Key benefits

  • Reduces joint pain and stiffness within 6–8 weeks of consistent practice
  • Strengthens supporting muscles, reducing joint load
  • Maintains range of motion and prevents deconditioning
  • Supports healthy weight and cardiovascular health
  • Improves mood, sleep, and energy levels

faqs.q: What are the best exercises for osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: The best exercises for osteoarthritis combine gentle range-of-motion work, strengthening of muscles around the affected joints, and low-impact aerobic activity such as walking, cycling or swimming. Start gradually and build up over several weeks.

faqs.q: Is it safe to exercise with oa?
faqs.a: Yes — for most people with oa, regular movement is one of the most effective self-management tools. Some short-term discomfort can be normal, but stop if you have sharp pain or sudden swelling and speak to a physiotherapist.

faqs.q: What exercises should I avoid with osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: Avoid high-impact activities that cause sharp joint pain, heavy loaded movements without proper preparation, and anything that triggers swelling lasting more than 24 hours. A physiotherapist can tailor a programme to your joints and goals.

faqs.q: How often should I exercise with oa?
faqs.a: Aim for short, regular sessions — most days of the week — rather than long, intense workouts. UK physiotherapy guidance suggests building up to around 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into manageable sessions.

faqs.q: Can exercise reduce osteoarthritis pain?
faqs.a: Yes — strong evidence shows that consistent exercise reduces pain, stiffness and fatigue in osteoarthritis, while improving sleep, mood and overall function. Benefits usually appear within 6–8 weeks of regular practice.

/conditions/osteoarthritis/diet.question: Diet for osteoarthritis
/conditions/osteoarthritis/diet.answer: There's no specific OA diet, but maintaining a healthy weight and following a Mediterranean-style eating pattern can reduce inflammation and joint pain.
/conditions/osteoarthritis/diet.bodyHtml:
There's no specific OA diet, but maintaining a healthy weight and following a Mediterranean-style eating pattern can reduce inflammation and joint pain.

Foods to favour

  • Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) two to three times a week for omega-3s
  • Extra-virgin olive oil as the main cooking fat
  • Colourful vegetables and fruit, especially leafy greens and berries
  • Wholegrains: oats, brown rice, wholemeal bread
  • Pulses, nuts, and seeds for plant protein and fibre

Foods to limit

  • Ultra-processed foods high in added sugar and refined flour
  • Sugary drinks and excess alcohol
  • Processed and red meats more than a few times per week
  • Foods high in saturated fat (deep-fried foods, pastries)

faqs.q: What is the best diet for osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: A Mediterranean-style anti-inflammatory diet is the most evidence-backed eating pattern for osteoarthritis. It emphasises vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, pulses, oily fish, olive oil, nuts and seeds, with limited ultra-processed food and sugar.

faqs.q: What foods should I avoid with oa?
faqs.a: Limit ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks, excess alcohol, and large amounts of red or processed meat. Many people also notice individual triggers — a short food diary can help you spot them.

faqs.q: Can diet reduce osteoarthritis inflammation?
faqs.a: Yes — an anti-inflammatory eating pattern, combined with maintaining a healthy weight, has been shown to reduce joint pain and inflammatory markers in osteoarthritis. Diet works best alongside exercise and any prescribed medication.

faqs.q: Do supplements help with oa?
faqs.a: Evidence is mixed. Omega-3 fish oil, vitamin D (where deficient), and turmeric/curcumin have the most supportive research for oa. Speak to your GP or pharmacist before starting supplements, especially if you take other medication.

faqs.q: Is there a single food that triggers osteoarthritis flares?
faqs.a: No single food causes osteoarthritis, but ultra-processed foods, excess sugar, and (for gout in particular) high-purine foods and alcohol can worsen symptoms. Focus on overall pattern rather than individual "miracle" or "forbidden" foods.

Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is an inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis. Around 150,000 people in the UK live with PsA, and roughly 1 in 5 people with psoriasis develop it.

Common symptoms of psoriatic arthritis

  • Joint pain and stiffness, often asymmetrical
  • Dactylitis — sausage-like swelling of a whole finger or toe
  • Nail changes: pitting, ridging, or separation from the nail bed
  • Lower back and buttock pain (axial involvement)
  • Enthesitis — pain where tendons attach to bone, especially at the heel
  • Fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance

When to see your GP

If you have psoriasis and develop joint pain, swelling, dactylitis, or persistent back stiffness, ask your GP about referral to rheumatology for screening.

/conditions/gout/symptoms.question: Gout symptoms
/conditions/gout/symptoms.answer: Gout is caused by sharp urate crystals forming in joints, leading to sudden, severe attacks. It affects around 1 in 40 adults in the UK and is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis in men.
/conditions/gout/symptoms.bodyHtml:
Gout is caused by sharp urate crystals forming in joints, leading to sudden, severe attacks. It affects around 1 in 40 adults in the UK and is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis in men.

Common symptoms of gout

  • Sudden onset of severe joint pain, often overnight or in the early morning
  • Hot, red, swollen joint — most commonly the base of the big toe
  • Skin over the joint may look shiny and peel as the attack settles
  • Even bedsheet pressure can feel unbearable during an attack
  • Attacks typically last 5–10 days and resolve fully between flares
  • Long-standing gout can cause visible lumps called tophi

When to see your GP

See your GP urgently during a first suspected attack to confirm the diagnosis. Book a routine appointment if you have repeated attacks to discuss long-term urate-lowering treatment.

faqs.q: What are the first signs of gout?
faqs.a: The earliest signs of gout often include joint pain, stiffness — particularly in the morning or after rest — and reduced flexibility in the affected area. Symptoms typically develop gradually, so keep a short symptom diary and speak to your GP if pain persists for more than a few weeks.

faqs.q: How is gout diagnosed in the UK?
faqs.a: In the UK, GPs diagnose gout from your symptoms, a clinical examination, and — where appropriate — blood tests, X-rays, ultrasound or MRI. For inflammatory types, your GP may refer you to UK healthcare rheumatology for specialist review under NICE guidance.

faqs.q: Can gout symptoms come and go?
faqs.a: Yes. Many people with gout experience flares — periods of worse pain, swelling and stiffness — followed by quieter spells. Tracking your flares helps you and your GP spot triggers and adjust treatment.

faqs.q: When should I see a GP about gout symptoms?
faqs.a: Book a GP appointment if joint pain has lasted more than a few weeks, is interfering with sleep or daily life, or is accompanied by swelling, warmth, locking or unexplained fatigue. Early assessment leads to better long-term outcomes.

faqs.q: Is gout the same as general arthritis pain?
faqs.a: No — there are over 100 forms of arthritis, and gout has its own pattern of symptoms, affected joints and treatment pathway. Getting the right diagnosis matters because the most effective treatments differ between conditions.

/conditions/gout/treatment.question: Gout treatment
/conditions/gout/treatment.answer: Gout treatment has two parts: managing the acute attack, and lowering uric acid long term to prevent further attacks and joint damage.
/conditions/gout/treatment.bodyHtml:
Gout treatment has two parts: managing the acute attack, and lowering uric acid long term to prevent further attacks and joint damage.

Treatment approaches

NSAIDs during attacks

First-line for most people — start as soon as the attack begins.

Colchicine

Effective for acute attacks, particularly if NSAIDs aren't suitable.

Short steroid course

Used when NSAIDs and colchicine aren't appropriate.

Allopurinol

Long-term urate-lowering therapy — the cornerstone of preventing future attacks.

Febuxostat

Alternative urate-lowering option when allopurinol isn't tolerated.

Lifestyle measures

Weight management, reduced alcohol, and good hydration alongside medication.

faqs.q: What is the best treatment for gout in the UK?
faqs.a: UK treatment for gout follows NICE guidance and usually combines self-management (exercise, weight control, pacing), pain relief, and — where needed — specialist medication or therapy. There is no single "best" option; the right plan depends on the type, severity and joints involved.

faqs.q: Can gout be cured?
faqs.a: Most forms of gout cannot be cured, but they can be very effectively managed. With the right combination of exercise, medication, and lifestyle support, many people maintain a full and active life.

faqs.q: What painkillers help gout?
faqs.a: Common options include paracetamol, topical or oral NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen) and, for inflammatory types, prescription medication such as DMARDs or biologics. Always take pain relief at the lowest effective dose and ask your GP or pharmacist about interactions.

faqs.q: Are there free UK healthcare resources for gout treatment?

/conditions/gout/exercises.bodyHtml:
Between attacks, regular non-weight-bearing exercise reduces gout flare frequency, supports healthy weight, and protects cardiovascular health.

Key benefits

  • Supports a healthy weight (a major factor in gout risk)
  • Improves circulation, helping the body clear uric acid
  • Reduces flare frequency over time
  • Protects cardiovascular health (gout is linked to heart disease)
  • Maintains joint function between attacks

faqs.q: What are the best exercises for gout?
faqs.a: The best exercises for gout combine gentle range-of-motion work, strengthening of muscles around the affected joints, and low-impact aerobic activity such as walking, cycling or swimming. Start gradually and build up over several weeks.

faqs.q: Is it safe to exercise with gout?
faqs.a: Yes — for most people with gout, regular movement is one of the most effective self-management tools. Some short-term discomfort can be normal, but stop if you have sharp pain or sudden swelling and speak to a physiotherapist.

faqs.q: What exercises should I avoid with gout?
faqs.a: Avoid high-impact activities that cause sharp joint pain, heavy loaded movements without proper preparation, and anything that triggers swelling lasting more than 24 hours. A physiotherapist can tailor a programme to your joints and goals.

faqs.q: How often should I exercise with gout?
faqs.a: Aim for short, regular sessions — most days of the week — rather than long, intense workouts. UK physiotherapy guidance suggests building up to around 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into manageable sessions.

faqs.q: Can exercise reduce gout pain?
faqs.a: Yes — strong evidence shows that consistent exercise reduces pain, stiffness and fatigue in gout, while improving sleep, mood and overall function. Benefits usually appear within 6–8 weeks of regular practice.

Foods to favour

  • Plenty of water (aim for 2 litres daily)
  • Low-fat dairy — protective against gout attacks
  • Cherries and cherry juice (modest evidence for reducing flares)
  • Coffee in moderation
  • Vegetables, wholegrains, and plant proteins

Foods to limit

  • Beer and spirits — strongly associated with attacks
  • Sugar-sweetened drinks and foods high in fructose
  • Organ meats (liver, kidney, sweetbreads)
  • Shellfish and oily fish in large amounts
  • Game meats and large amounts of red meat

faqs.q: What foods should I avoid with gout?

Common symptoms of fibromyalgia

  • Widespread pain lasting more than three months

  • Sleep that doesn't feel restorative
  • Heightened sensitivity to touch, light, sound, or temperature
  • Irritable bowel symptoms, headaches, and mood changes

faqs.q: What foods should I avoid with pmr?
faqs.a: Limit ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks, excess alcohol, and large amounts of red or processed meat. Many people also notice individual triggers — a short food diary can help you spot them.

faqs.q: Can diet reduce polymyalgia rheumatica inflammation?
faqs.a: Yes — an anti-inflammatory eating pattern, combined with maintaining a healthy weight, has been shown to reduce joint pain and inflammatory markers in polymyalgia rheumatica. Diet works best alongside exercise and any prescribed medication.

faqs.q: Do supplements help with pmr?
faqs.a: Evidence is mixed. Omega-3 fish oil, vitamin D (where deficient), and turmeric/curcumin have the most supportive research for pmr. Speak to your GP or pharmacist before starting supplements, especially if you take other medication.

faqs.q: Is there a single food that triggers polymyalgia rheumatica flares?
faqs.a: No single food causes polymyalgia rheumatica, but ultra-processed foods, excess sugar, and (for gout in particular) high-purine foods and alcohol can worsen symptoms. Focus on overall pattern rather than individual "miracle" or "forbidden" foods.

/conditions/reactive-arthritis/symptoms.answer: Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation triggered by an infection elsewhere in the body — usually a gut or urinary infection. Symptoms typically appear 2–4 weeks after the triggering infection.
/conditions/reactive-arthritis/symptoms.bodyHtml:
Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation triggered by an infection elsewhere in the body — usually a gut or urinary infection. Symptoms typically appear 2–4 weeks after the triggering infection.

Common symptoms of reactive arthritis

  • Joint pain and swelling, often in the knees, ankles, or feet
  • Lower back or buttock pain
  • Heel pain (enthesitis)
  • Dactylitis — sausage-like swelling of a toe or finger
  • Eye inflammation (conjunctivitis or uveitis)
  • Burning on passing urine, even after the triggering infection has cleared

When to see your GP

See your GP if you develop joint pain and swelling within a few weeks of a gut or urinary infection. Mention the recent infection — it's an important clue for diagnosis.

faqs.q: What are the first signs of reactive arthritis?
faqs.a: The earliest signs of reactive arthritis often include joint pain, stiffness — particularly in the morning or after rest — and reduced flexibility in the affected area. Symptoms typically develop gradually, so keep a short symptom diary and speak to your GP if pain persists for more than a few weeks.

faqs.q: How is reactive arthritis diagnosed in the UK?
faqs.a: In the UK, GPs diagnose reactive arthritis from your symptoms, a clinical examination, and — where appropriate — blood tests, X-rays, ultrasound or MRI. For inflammatory types, your GP may refer you to UK healthcare rheumatology for specialist review under NICE guidance.

faqs.q: Can rea symptoms come and go?
faqs.a: Yes. Many people with rea experience flares — periods of worse pain, swelling and stiffness — followed by quieter spells. Tracking your flares helps you and your GP spot triggers and adjust treatment.

faqs.q: When should I see a GP about reactive arthritis symptoms?
faqs.a: Book a GP appointment if joint pain has lasted more than a few weeks, is interfering with sleep or daily life, or is accompanied by swelling, warmth, locking or unexplained fatigue. Early assessment leads to better long-term outcomes.

faqs.q: Is reactive arthritis the same as general arthritis pain?
faqs.a: No — there are over 100 forms of arthritis, and reactive arthritis has its own pattern of symptoms, affected joints and treatment pathway. Getting the right diagnosis matters because the most effective treatments differ between conditions.

/conditions/reactive-arthritis/treatment.question: Reactive arthritis treatment
/conditions/reactive-arthritis/treatment.answer: Most cases of reactive arthritis resolve within 6 months. Treatment focuses on symptom control, managing the triggering infection if still present, and preventing joint damage in persistent cases.
/conditions/reactive-arthritis/treatment.bodyHtml:
Most cases of reactive arthritis resolve within 6 months. Treatment focuses on symptom control, managing the triggering infection if still present, and preventing joint damage in persistent cases.

Treatment approaches

NSAIDs

First-line for joint pain and stiffness.

Steroid joint injections

Helpful for individually swollen joints.

Antibiotics

Used to treat the triggering infection if still active (not for the arthritis itself).

Sulfasalazine or methotrexate

Considered for persistent disease lasting beyond 6 months.

Physiotherapy

Maintains range of motion and helps return to normal activity.

Eye and skin review

Ophthalmology and dermatology input if eyes, skin, or nails are involved.

faqs.q: What is the best treatment for reactive arthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: UK treatment for reactive arthritis follows NICE guidance and usually combines self-management (exercise, weight control, pacing), pain relief, and — where needed — specialist medication or therapy. There is no single "best" option; the right plan depends on the type, severity and joints involved.

faqs.q: Can reactive arthritis be cured?
faqs.a: Most forms of rea cannot be cured, but they can be very effectively managed. With the right combination of exercise, medication, and lifestyle support, many people maintain a full and active life.

faqs.q: What painkillers help reactive arthritis?
faqs.a: Common options include paracetamol, topical or oral NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen) and, for inflammatory types, prescription medication such as DMARDs or biologics. Always take pain relief at the lowest effective dose and ask your GP or pharmacist about interactions.

faqs.q: Do I need a referral to see a rheumatologist for rea?
faqs.a: Yes — in the UK, you'll usually need a referral from your GP to access UK healthcare rheumatology services. If your GP suspects an inflammatory arthritis, NICE recommends urgent referral so that treatment can start early.

faqs.q: Are there free UK healthcare resources for reactive arthritis treatment?
faqs.a: Yes. UK healthcare physiotherapy, occupational therapy, pain clinics and self-management programmes are available — many free at the point of use. Ask your GP or check the UK healthcare system website for services in your area.

/conditions/reactive-arthritis/exercises.answer: Gentle low-impact exercise during recovery helps restore joint mobility and prevents deconditioning while the underlying inflammation resolves.
/conditions/reactive-arthritis/exercises.bodyHtml:
Gentle low-impact exercise during recovery helps restore joint mobility and prevents deconditioning while the underlying inflammation resolves.

Key benefits

  • Maintains joint range of motion during recovery
  • Prevents deconditioning
  • Supports return to normal activity
  • Improves mood and energy
  • Helps with persistent enthesitis (heel and tendon pain)

faqs.q: What are the best exercises for reactive arthritis?
faqs.a: The best exercises for reactive arthritis combine gentle range-of-motion work, strengthening of muscles around the affected joints, and low-impact aerobic activity such as walking, cycling or swimming. Start gradually and build up over several weeks.

faqs.q: Is it safe to exercise with rea?
faqs.a: Yes — for most people with rea, regular movement is one of the most effective self-management tools. Some short-term discomfort can be normal, but stop if you have sharp pain or sudden swelling and speak to a physiotherapist.

faqs.q: What exercises should I avoid with reactive arthritis?
faqs.a: Avoid high-impact activities that cause sharp joint pain, heavy loaded movements without proper preparation, and anything that triggers swelling lasting more than 24 hours. A physiotherapist can tailor a programme to your joints and goals.

faqs.q: How often should I exercise with rea?
faqs.a: Aim for short, regular sessions — most days of the week — rather than long, intense workouts. UK physiotherapy guidance suggests building up to around 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into manageable sessions.

faqs.q: Can exercise reduce reactive arthritis pain?
faqs.a: Yes — strong evidence shows that consistent exercise reduces pain, stiffness and fatigue in reactive arthritis, while improving sleep, mood and overall function. Benefits usually appear within 6–8 weeks of regular practice.

Foods to limit

  • Anything that personally upsets your gut
